thread.title: How consumer companies can thrive in the age of millennials

author: Doug Straton
title: How consumer companies can thrive in the age of millennials
text:
One of the most popular toys on the market this past holiday season was something called L.O.L. Surprise! The line of small dolls that children can collect and dress in various outfits flew off the shelves.
But the unique thing about the dolls isn’t what they wear, but how they are packaged. Rather than a typical box, each doll comes inside a large plastic ball that contains up to a dozen layers of different “surprises,” including stickers, charms, outfits and other accessories.
The experience of opening this package is a large part of the appeal. Videos of exhilarated children opening each ball are generating millions of views on YouTube, which is also integrated into their brand site and has all manner of interactive features, printouts and “collectibles,” bolstered by the highly downloaded “L.O.L. Surprise Ball Pop” apps.
There may be no better metaphor for companies looking to connect with millennials (and clearly, their children). Today, how this generation experiences, communicates and shares information about products is in many ways more important than the product itself, and critical to brand building.
Yesterday’s shopping experiences are no longer relevant. With our devices, we’re summoning rides through Uber, ordering groceries online via smart lists, subscribing to and binge-watching our TV shows through Netflix NFLX, -5.47% Everything is on-demand, everything is personalized and everything is available right now. And when we like our experiences, we share with those we care about.
The lesson here: You’d better understand, authentically connect to, interact, serve — and, yes, trust your consumers with your brand. That’s how you’ll be able to deliver value and loyalty. It is this reality that is driving three major interrelated changes in retail.
Personalization through experience 
Millennials prefer offerings that feel unique to them as individuals rather than something that is generic or appeals to everyone. That said, the products themselves don’t need to be customized to each individual. Products that feel personalized, through the experience of buying it reflect a company that knows how to communicate with its consumers and understands what they want.
This can happen instantly and at scale through devices, driven by data about you and only you. The brands that have the most information about how people engage with their offerings and know how to weaponize that data through advanced analytics are going to be most likely to get personalized experiences right and drive value for both the consumer and the brand. For example, the way Apple approaches design and marketing, and the way it delivers on its value proposition are all about simplifying the complex and allowing individualism and self-expression. Nothing is more personal – or personalized — than what you experience and share through your phone. Apple’s AAPL, -2.75% advertising reflects this.
Deep connections between people and their preferred brands are becoming table stakes, not just for technology companies, but because of them. Consumers have been trained to expect personal, expect easy, and expect service.
Products as experiential services 
Tightly connected to personalization through experience is the blurring between what we traditionally think of as a “product” manufactured by a brand and what we think of as a “service.” Unlike products, services can be improved and updated 24/7, at relatively low cost. Again, we can thank the progressively higher capability and lower costs of advanced digital solutions for this.
Sun Basket is a great example. A meal-kit delivery service with vegetarian, gluten-free and paleo offerings, the company studies its data to sharpen its offerings, creating highly personalized — even if not entirely customized — recipes. It can easily extend this service platform to provide new sources of growth and ways to serve an already loyal customer base.
Or consider Thrive Market, which at first appears to simply be an organic e-commerce retailer. A deeper look shows that Thrive is actually selling a lifestyle with a robust business intelligence unit and an in-house content production team. It caters very specifically to its customers’ behavior and feedback, particularly around the importance of a shared social mission. Its product sales enable this, but Thrive’s proposition can stretch to other lifestyle choices beyond organic food.
It’s less about what you’re selling and more about making sure that you’re maximizing every single occasion for people to use your offering as opposed to others.
Millennials are the first generation that is truly primed for this reality, and they’re starting to expect it from the companies they buy from. Soon, I expect to see just about every brand having a service component to their offerings.
People trust people 
In the era of “fake news” it is perhaps not surprising that studies indicate that people trust other people more than they do brands. Due to the explosion of devices, people now create more information about brands and products, both good and bad, than any one company could possibly create themselves. Increasingly, this means the only way for brands to authentically reach people is to focus on how people are talking about their offerings to others, and to use this as a means of connecting with them.
To be sure, a carefully crafted brand proposition is still key, but now in many ways your brand is really what people say it is when you are not in the room. Harness user-generated content and use it in your marketing strategy. Understand how the true perception of your brand (is it even yours anymore?) can positively drive how people search for, interact with and buy your products. Develop relationships and listen to your consumers. They’ll tell you what they want.
The time is now to invest in the new technologies that will make these insights possible and actionable. Companies that ignore these changes and hold on to the marketing tactics of the past increasingly do so at their own peril.
Doug Straton is Chief Digital Commerce Officer at The Hershey Co .
